title: Blackcurrant Cordial
subtitle: Deep, sharp, intensely purple, the British summer cordial
excerpt: Blackcurrant cordial is made by simmering fresh blackcurrants with sugar and water, then straining. Intensely flavoured and deeply purple. Makes about 1.5 litres of concentrate.
sourceNotes: Pam Corbin, Preserves. Blackcurrant cordial is the homemade equivalent of Ribena. Fresh blackcurrants have 4× the vitamin C of oranges and a deeply distinctive flavour.

recipe.yieldDescription: Makes about 1.5 litres of cordial (dilute 1:8 to 1:10)
recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in ice cube trays for up to 12 months.

content.text: Blackcurrant cordial tastes like the best version of Ribena,  deeply fruity, sharply acidic, and vivid purple. The fresh currants are simmered briefly with sugar and water, then the juice is strained out. No long cooking,  heat destroys some of the vitamin C and dulls the colour. Makes about 1.5 litres of concentrate.

items.prepNote: fresh or defrosted frozen, stalks removed
brightens the flavour and helps preserve

content.text: Put the blackcurrants and water in a large saucepan. Bring to a simmer and cook gently for 10 minutes, pressing the currants against the side of the pan to help them release their juice. The fruit should collapse completely.

Pour through a fine sieve into a large jug, pressing firmly on the pulp to extract as much juice as possible. Return the juice to the cleaned pan. Add the sugar and lemon juice and stir over low heat until the sugar dissolves completely. Do not boil at this stage,  you want the sugar dissolved, not the juice reduced.
Pour the hot cordial into hot sterilised bottles and seal immediately. The heat seals the bottle and extends shelf life. Leave to cool.

items.cause: Cooked too long or at too high a temperature.
items.fix: Keep to a gentle simmer, 10 minutes is enough. Prolonged heat dulls the vivid purple pigment.

items.cause: Reduced too much when dissolving the sugar.
items.fix: The sugar should dissolve off the boil or at a very low heat. Avoid reducing the cordial.

items.cause: Not hot enough when bottled, or bottles not sterilised.
items.fix: Bottle while the cordial is still hot (above 85 °C) into hot sterilised bottles. Refrigerate after opening.

items.symptom: Seeds or pulp in the finished cordial
items.fix: Line the sieve with muslin. Blackcurrant seeds are small and need a fine mesh to catch them.

content.text: Sealed bottles: 3 to 4 weeks in the fridge. Freeze for up to 12 months.
